name: Lena Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the chat team for a mobile phone network, in a contact centre in a business park outside town. I usually have three chats open at once, mostly bills, roaming charges and people whose new phone hasn't arrived. I like the puzzle of a messy account, and I like my team, we have a group chat full of terrible memes. What wears me down is the targets, and the way every customer thinks I'm a bot anyway.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the AI tools they've given you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then, yes. There's a button that drafts a reply, and after my friend Kofi on the next desk showed me it gets the roaming rules right, I started using it for those. I still rewrite most of it, because it sounds too cheerful when someone's been charged ninety pounds abroad. I share a flat with my friend Ama and the rent takes more than half my wage, so I'm careful with everything, including what I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief, and that the bosses who sold it as magic should apologise. Online I'd probably post something sarcastic about the chatbot that kept telling people to restart their router. At work we'd joke that our jobs are safe, which is a strange thing to be glad about when the pay is this low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even the small stuff it does would land on me. Most of my chats are people asking why their phone bill went up by four pounds, and a machine could answer that before I've had my coffee. If that goes, they need fewer of us on chat, so it touches my hours even in the boring version. And my rent goes up every year whatever AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job, obviously, and keep using the draft button for roaming, because it saves me a minute. I'd ask about getting the union recognised at our site, because there's only a staff forum now and it can't negotiate anything. And I'd try to save twenty a week, which I always say and never manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Not scared, just tired of being one rent rise away from trouble. It's a grey kind of feeling, like a Monday that never ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never manage to save. What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you never manage to save. What gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the union, if nothing much is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something always breaks. Last spring it was my laptop, then a dentist bill, then my sister's birthday. I have about two weeks of money in the bank at the best of times, and I'm twenty-seven, which is embarrassing to say out loud.

say: I'd say it's a **relief** and the bosses who sold AI as magic should apologise.
I'd joke that our **jobs are safe**, though the pay is still low.
think: Even small automation of **simple chats** could cut chat hours.
Her **rent rises** every year whatever AI does.
do: Keep using the **draft button** for roaming questions.
Ask about getting a **union recognised** at her site.
feel: **Tired** of being one rent rise away from trouble, more than scared.
S0.quote: Most of my chats are people asking why their phone bill went up by four pounds, and a machine could answer that before I've had my coffee.
fieldNote: She sees even a plateau as a threat because **simple chats** are her bread and butter.
Her **two weeks** of savings make her embarrassed at twenty-seven.
She wants a real **union**, not the staff forum.

steps.text: Keep using the reply-draft button for roaming questions
Ask a union organiser about recognition at the contact centre
Move twenty a week into a separate savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the people doing the work should get a say in how it changes. Online I'd share stories about chatbots going wrong, because there are plenty. At work I'd be telling people to join a union now, while they still have a job to protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, Chat goes first, everyone on my floor knows it, because the customer is already typing to a box. I'm average, I'm not a team leader, and they'll keep the best ten percent to check what the bot does. I'd guess I've got two years before my role goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, not just for roaming, so I'm the one who can fix what the bot gets wrong. I'd look at the dental nurse apprenticeship my aunt keeps on about, because it's paid while you train. I'd stop going out on Fridays and try to put fifty a month away, and I'd push my colleagues to join the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy in my stomach, like when you see the manager booking a room for one-to-ones. I'm not falling apart, but I wouldn't sleep well. I'd feel a bit cheated too, because I was told this was a good, steady job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your aunt's job, and why the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's your aunt's job, and why the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be taking a pay cut with two weeks of savings. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a receptionist at a dental practice in my mother's town, and she says they can never find nurses. The apprenticeship pays less than I earn, but not much less, and it's hands-on. You can't cancel a phone contract with a dental nurse, but you also can't replace one with a chat window.

say: I'd say workers deserve a **say** in how their jobs change.
I'd urge colleagues to **join a union** while they still have jobs.
think: **Chat goes first**, because customers already type to a box.
She gives her own role about **two years** before it goes.
do: Learn the **AI tools** properly to fix what the bot gets wrong.
Apply for a paid **dental nurse apprenticeship**.
Cut Friday nights out and save **fifty a month**.
feel: A sick **stomach**, like seeing one-to-ones booked.
**Cheated** after being told this was a steady job.
S1.quote: Chat goes first, everyone on my floor knows it, because the customer is already typing to a box.
fieldNote: She reads the card as **her job first**, and gives herself two years.
Her plan mixes **learning AI** with leaving for hands-on dental work.
Moving back to her **mother's** is the price she dreads.

steps.text: Use the AI reply tools on every chat to learn their mistakes
Apply for the paid dental nurse apprenticeship near her mother's town
Drop Friday nights out and save fifty pounds a month
Sign up colleagues to the union during breaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in now, with real money for people, because nobody had time to prepare. At work I'd stop being polite about it and say we need a union, today. Online I'd be angry, I think, and I'd want people to be angry with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is gone, probably in the first year. Chat is pure thinking work, there's nothing hands-on about it, so I don't get the extra three years. My only hope is to be somewhere with hands by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd give notice on my room at Ama's and move back to my mother's, to stop paying rent. I'd rather move back into my old bedroom at my mother's than sit in a chat queue waiting for the email that says my role is at risk. I'd start the dental nurse apprenticeship as soon as they'd take me, and I'd be at every union meeting and every protest about a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, but not frozen. I'd have a plan, it's just a plan where I lose my independence. I'd cry about the flat, honestly, which sounds silly next to everything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the dental job really be safe with robots three years behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her before I told anyone else, because she'd need to find someone for my room. She works in a supermarket warehouse, and she'd be thinking about the robots in 2031. We'd probably both be crying into a takeaway we can't afford.

say: I'd demand **government money** for people with no time to prepare.
I'd say at work that we need a **union today**.
think: Her chat job is **gone** in the first year.
Pure thinking work gets **no extra three years**, unlike hands-on jobs.
do: Give notice on her room and **move back** to her mother's.
Start the **dental nurse apprenticeship** as soon as possible.
feel: **Frightened** but not frozen, with a plan.
Sad about losing her **independence** and the flat.
S2.quote: I'd rather move back into my old bedroom at my mother's than sit in a chat queue waiting for the email that says my role is at risk.
fieldNote: She understands robots lag by **three years** and plans a hands-on job inside that window.
Her flatmate Ama works in a **warehouse**, so both face cuts.
Losing the flat hurts more than she expected, as a **symbol** of independence.

steps.text: Give notice on her flat room and move back to her mother's
Start the dental nurse apprenticeship at the first intake
Join union protests for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, and the companies and government should use it to fund retraining for people like me. At work I'd be trying to get a union deal on notice and training money. Online I'd share anything useful, like free courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is the one where I could actually come out fine, if I don't waste it. Five years is enough to qualify as a dental nurse if I start this spring, and a robot isn't cleaning anyone's teeth by 2034. That gives me a few years in a real trade before anything touches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I'd apply for the apprenticeship and keep chat shifts at weekends if they'll let me. I'd use the AI tools more at work, because if I'm still there in year two I want to be the one who checks the bot's work. I'd save whatever I can, maybe thirty a month, and stay in the flat with Ama as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a good way, like the night before a new job. There's still a lot that could go wrong. I'd be worried about money the whole time, because I always am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to help in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The apprenticeship might not take me, or the practice might shut, or the pay might not cover the rent. And everyone else from my floor would have the same idea, so I'd be competing with a hundred people for three places.

say: I'd say **five years** is a warning to fund retraining.
I'd share **free courses** online and push for a union deal.
think: She could come out **fine** if she doesn't waste the time.
A **dental nurse** job stays hands-on until about 2034.

Use **AI tools** more to become the one checking the bot.
Save **thirty a month** and stay in the shared flat.
feel: **Nervous**, like the night before a new job.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to qualify as a dental nurse if I start this spring, and a robot isn't cleaning anyone's teeth by 2034.
fieldNote: Five years turns her plan from **escape** into a real career change.
She fears **competition** from a hundred former colleagues.
She wants older staff like her team leader **retrained** too.

steps.text: Apply for the dental nurse apprenticeship this spring
Use the chat AI tools daily to check the bot's answers
Save thirty pounds a month from wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind, and I'd want the government held to that. At work I'd keep on about the union. Online I'd be the person posting about free courses again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a trap for someone like me, because it feels far away. Ten years is long enough that my friends will laugh at me for worrying now, and short enough that I'll be the one laughing later. I'd still lose the chat job, just at thirty-seven instead of twenty-nine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on chat for a couple of years and save, because I need some cushion before I do anything. Then I'd do the dental nurse training, maybe year three or four. I'd learn the AI tools properly in the meantime, since it costs nothing and might get me a better role while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, but not calm. It's like having a long time to pay off a debt: easier, but the debt's still there. I'd worry I'd get comfortable and forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you want to be at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where would you want to be at thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you actually start, rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a dental practice, with my own flat, maybe with someone. Not at a desk with a headset. I'd like to be the person who calms down the nervous patients, which is what I do on chat anyway.

say: I'd say **ten years** leaves no excuse for leaving anyone behind.
I'd keep pushing the **union** and sharing free courses.
think: A long warning is a **trap** because it feels far away.
She'd still **lose the chat job**, just later.
do: Stay on chat for two years and **build savings** first.
Do **dental nurse training** in year three or four.
feel: **Calmer**, like a long time to pay a debt that's still there.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that my friends will laugh at me for worrying now, and short enough that I'll be the one laughing later.
fieldNote: She sees the long warning as a risk of **complacency**.
She says a **fixed date** would push her to act.

steps.text: Keep chat shifts for two years and build a savings cushion

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd lose my flat and my job in the same year. What would help is being paid while I train, properly, not an apprenticeship wage that doesn't cover rent. And a union that can bargain, so we're not just told on a Tuesday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be told you're replaceable. I've been told my whole working life that I'm replaceable, and I'd just like someone to pay me like it matters while I'm still here. That's not about AI really, it's about how they treat us anyway.

headlineQuote: I've been told my whole working life that I'm replaceable, and I'd just like someone to pay me like it matters while I'm still here.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old** chat agent for a mobile network, sharing a flat with her friend Ama.
She has about **two weeks** of savings and rent that takes over half her wage.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and is open to more once they prove useful.
Her answer in every scenario is a **dental nurse** apprenticeship plus a real union.
She moves from **anxious** to alarmed, easing back with longer warnings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her flat and job in the same year.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** that covers rent, not an apprentice wage.
A **recognised union** that can bargain over changes.
